findings.committee: Children and Young People Services Scrutiny Committee
findings.paper_title: Covering Report
findings.headline: Net budget overspend of £3.4m driven by increased social care demand and failed savings delivery
findings.detail: The council delivered a net overspend of £3.4m in 2025-26, attributed to increased service demand (particularly in children's and adult social care) and delays or failures in delivering approved budget savings. This represents a concrete execution failure in financial management.
findings.matters: A material overspend in a major service directorate signals budget control problems and pressure from demand that exceeds the council's savings capacity—both material risks for lenders assessing financial stability.
findings.figures: £3.4m net budget overspend for the year
findings.quote: The Council continues to face severe financial pressures as a result of increased service demand (particularly within children's and adult social care) and delays/failure to deliver some of the approved budget savings which resulted in a net budget overspend of £3.4m for the year.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Appendix 1 St Helens_Area_SEND_Full_inspection_Feb26_
findings.headline: No commissioned special school nursing service in St Helens creates unmet statutory health need and cost gap
findings.detail: The council does not commission a special school nursing service; as a result, pupils are leaving school during the day to access health support elsewhere, and education staff lack clarity on health services' oversight of children in special schools. Outreach from paediatric services also lacks consistency across the area.
findings.matters: Unmet statutory duty creates safeguarding liability and will likely require the council to commission or self-fund a service to plug the gap, generating unbudgeted cost.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: The lack of a commissioned special school nursing service in St Helen's leaves practitioners and families uncertain about where health support is accessed by children in special school settings. Some children are leaving school during the day to access health support, impacting their education, and there is lack of clarity from education staff on health services' oversight of children in special schools.

findings.matters: Leadership transitions during service crises increase execution risk; a new director managing multiple systemic failures under Ofsted monitoring creates timeline uncertainty.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Appendix 1 St Helens_Area_SEND_Full_inspection_Feb26_
findings.headline: Council commissions only a single provider for all alternative education provision, creating concentration risk
findings.detail: St Helens has no backup alternative provision (AP) provider for excluded or vulnerable pupils; all provision comes from one commissioned provider. The inspection noted widespread delays and fragmentation across pathways that put pressure on this single arrangement.
findings.matters: Failure or withdrawal of the sole provider would create immediate statutory breach, leave vulnerable pupils unsupported, and force emergency unbudgeted procurement.
findings.figures: None given
findings.quote: The local authority commissions a single provider to deliver education for children and young people who cannot attend school due to social, emotional, mental health or medical needs, as well as those at risk of, or permanently excluded from, mainstream education. No other alternative provision (AP) is commissioned by the local authority.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - Appendix 1 St Helens_Area_SEND_Full_inspection_Feb26_
findings.headline: Ofsted found widespread and systemic failings in SEND services requiring urgent priority action plan
findings.detail: The inspection identified systemic weaknesses across mental health pathways, neurodevelopmental assessment (autism/ADHD), EHC plan processes, and short breaks provision. The inspection outcome requires the council and NHS to prepare a priority action plan urgently, with a monitoring inspection within approximately 18 months and full reinspection within 3 years.
findings.matters: A finance director must budget and resource the mandatory remediation programme on a compressed timeline; systemic failures suggest broader management or capacity issues.
findings.figures: Approximately 18 months to monitoring inspection; 3 years to full reinspection
findings.quote: There are widespread and/or systemic failings leading to significant concerns about the experiences and outcomes of children and young people with special educational needs and/or disabilities (SEND), which the local area partnership must address urgently. His Majesty's Chief Inspector requires the local area partnership to prepare and submit a priority action plan (area SEND) to address the identified areas for priority action.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Cabinet Report Housing Enforcement Policy Aug26
findings.headline: Training and system costs include unfunded future demand beyond initial government support
findings.detail: While initial training is funded by MHCLG, the council will face 'refresher and specialist training' costs that create 'future unfunded demand.' Additional unfunded costs include operational costs, case management systems, legal evidence bundles, and statutory government reporting requirements.
findings.matters: These hidden costs, not yet budgeted, add to the financial uncertainty around implementing the new duty and suggest the true cost of compliance may exceed current estimates.
findings.figures: None provided

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Cabinet Report Housing Enforcement Policy Aug26
findings.headline: Future income is explicitly uncertain and ring-fenced, unable to offset costs across the wider council
findings.detail: The council expects income from a Private Rented Sector database (due 'late 2026') and civil penalties to offset costs over time. However, the report explicitly states this income 'is dependent on actual levels of enforcement activity, landlord compliance and the outcome of appeals, it is uncertain and cannot be guaranteed.' Critically, civil penalty income 'must be reinvested solely into housing enforcement and cannot be used to offset wider service pressures.'
findings.matters: The council cannot rely on uncertain enforcement income to balance its budget, and cannot redirect it to help with other pressures, meaning all new costs must be absorbed from existing budgets or new funding sources.
findings.figures: Database fees from 'late 2026' (timing and amount not specified); no figures given for expected penalty income
findings.quote: As this income is dependent on actual levels of enforcement activity, landlord compliance and the outcome of appeals, it is uncertain and cannot be guaranteed. Civil penalty income must be reinvested solely into housing enforcement and cannot be used to offset wider service pressures.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Cabinet Report Housing Enforcement Policy Aug26
findings.headline: Council acknowledges explicit risk of net financial deficit from the new duties, with no clear funding solution identified
findings.detail: The report states 'there is a risk that the implementation of the new statutory duties may result in a net financial impact for the Council, particularly during the transition phase and until related income stabilises.' Rather than securing funding now, the council plans to manage implications through 'annual budget monitoring process.' Staffing resources are to be 'subject to separate approval' and funded from 'existing resources or new funding sources' (neither identified).
findings.matters: This signals the council has not solved the funding gap for a statutory obligation and may need to reallocate budgets or access reserves to meet a legal requirement it cannot refuse.
findings.figures: Transition phase timeline unspecified; income dependent on 'actual levels of enforcement activity, landlord compliance and the outcome of appeals'
findings.quote: Overall, while income streams will support the service over time, there is a risk that the implementation of the new statutory duties may result in a net financial impact for the Council, particularly during the transition phase and until related income stabilises. In the first instance, the service will look to deal with the financial implications as part of annual budget monitoring process.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - Cabinet Report Housing Enforcement Policy Aug26
findings.headline: New mandatory enforcement duties creating additional staffing costs across multiple services without confirmed funding
findings.detail: The Renters' Rights Act 2025 imposes new statutory duties requiring the council to add capacity across Private Sector Housing, Legal Services, Customer Services, Housing Options and Finance. The report acknowledges this will introduce 'new and ongoing financial pressures' and 'increased staffing costs' that must be considered in future budget planning, but does not specify how much or where the funding will come from.
findings.matters: This is a new, unfunded mandate that will increase the council's cost base. A lender needs to know if the council has reserve capacity to absorb these costs or whether it will require budget reallocation, reserve drawdown, or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: None provided for staffing costs; new private rented sector of 12,264 properties in borough
findings.quote: The Act places mandatory enforcement duties on the authority, meaning additional capacity will be required across Private Sector Housing, Legal Services, Customer Services, Housing Options and Finance. The implementation of the Renters' Rights Act 2025 will introduce new and ongoing financial pressures for the Council. This will result in increased staffing costs, which will need to be considered in future budget planning.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Property disposal (Lincoln and Wesley House) delayed, losing £0.136m saving and creating ongoing £0.113m rental income pressure
findings.detail: The planned rationalisation and disposal of Lincoln and Wesley House has not been achieved, creating a £0.136m pressure from delayed savings. The Cabinet report seeking approval for disposal has been deferred to Autumn. Even when the disposal occurs, it will result in a loss of rental income creating 'an ongoing pressure of (£0.113m) that will need to be addressed as part of future financial planning.'
findings.matters: This is a relatively modest sum, but it illustrates asset management delays creating both near-term savings slippage and permanent structural revenue loss. Deferred property disposals often signal underlying issues with asset valuation, demand, or decision-making speed.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement costs rising 16-21% over two years; dependency on price stabilisation continuing
findings.detail: The council reports that 'the average price of a supported living placement has risen by 21% in the last two years. Similarly, the average price of a package of residential and nursing care has risen by 17% and 16% respectively, over the same time period.' While the report notes 'most of that increase was incurred in the 2024-2025 financial year, with price rises flattening off during since mid-2025,' the Adult Social Care portfolio is forecast to balance only 'based on the assumption that sufficient measures will be put in place to manage the increasing demand.' The portfolio faces £4.4m in unaddressed demand pressures.
findings.matters: Care placement cost inflation at this scale (16-21% over 2 years) far exceeds general inflation and cannot be sustained indefinitely. The council is managing this year by assuming it can hold price growth flat, but this is fragile and dependent on market conditions. Further price inflation would force either additional budget pressure or service reduction.
findings.figures: Supported living up 21% in 2 years; residential/nursing care up 17% and 16%; £4.4m unaddressed demand pressure; nursing care numbers +6% since February 2026; CHC funding down 19%
findings.quote: The average price of a supported living placement has risen by 21% in the last two years. Similarly, the average price of a package of residential and nursing care has risen by 17% and 16% respectively, over the same time period. Left unaddressed, the increasing demand for social care is forecast to cost the department £4.4m in 2026-2027.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Medium-term budget gap of £6.8m in 2028/29 with core spending power growth of only 1.3-1.5%
findings.detail: Under the three-year finance settlement, the council's core spending power is forecast to grow only 1.3% in 2027/28 and 1.5% in 2028/29, compared to the English average of 4.3% and 4.4%. A budget gap of £6.8m is forecast for 2028/29. Directorates have been tasked with finding efficiencies of 1.5% per annum to meet the shortfall, but this is separate from the current year overspend.
findings.matters: St Helens is facing a significantly worse funding trajectory than its peers. Combined with current-year overspending and a structural SEND funding problem, the 2028/29 position represents a medium-term affordability challenge that will require either major service cuts or additional reserves use.
findings.figures: £6.8m forecast budget gap 2028/29; core spending power growth 1.3% (2027/28) and 1.5% (2028/29); English average 4.3% and 4.4%; 1.5% efficiency target per annum required
findings.quote: The quantum of funding that the Council is currently predicted to receive reduces in the final two years of the Settlement period. The additional funding helped to achieve a balanced budget this year and for next year. However, there is a forecast budget gap in the final year of the settlement period 2028/29 of £6.8m. Directorates have been tasked with finding efficiencies equivalent to 1.5% of the budget per annum to meet the current shortfall within the Medium Term Financial Strategy.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: £90m capital borrowing requirement deferred due to high rates and challenging financial position
findings.detail: The council identified a need to borrow approximately £90m to fund its capital programme and regeneration schemes. However, it has 'previously deferred any additional capital investment funded by borrowing' due to 'increased cost of borrowing and the Council's challenging financial position.' In July 2026, it secured only £5m temporary borrowing at 4.65% for 1 year as a stop-gap, stating it will 'continue to review its cashflow position and the forecast for interest rate movements to identify the most opportune moment to take out any borrowing.' This defers major capital investment decisions.
findings.matters: Deferring £90m of planned capital borrowing signals financial stress. While rate management is normal, deferring capital investment due to both cost and financial position suggests the council may not be able to afford the borrowing even at better rates. This is a concern for service delivery and sustainability.
findings.figures: £90m capital borrowing requirement; £5m secured July 2026 at 4.65% for 1 year; approximately £85m still deferred
findings.quote: When setting the budget, the need to borrow a significant amount of circa £90m to fund the Council's capital programme and committed regeneration schemes in the current year was assumed. In light of the increased cost of borrowing and the Council's challenging financial position, the Council has previously deferred any additional capital investment funded by borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund balances forecast to fall £5.617m to £8.983m, below prudent level of £14.6m
findings.detail: The council's General Fund balance is forecast to drop from a planned £14.6m target to £8.983m by 31 March 2027 — a shortfall of £5.617m. The report states that 'if the financial position can be brought back to a balanced position or better, this will be the first year since 2021/22 that the transfer of earmarked reserves to maintain the general fund at a prudent level (£14.6m from 2026/27) will not be required.' It then warns: 'if the trend of previous years continues the use of earmarked reserves will again be necessary in 2026/27 to replenish general fund balances.'
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's shock absorber. Repeated drawdowns to cover revenue overspends (rather than one-off items) signal that revenue spending is unsustainable. Five years of this pattern is unsustainable. A lender reviews reserves as liquidity and affordability cover.
findings.figures: £14.6m prudent target; £8.983m forecast 31 March 2027; £5.617m drawdown; 5 successive years of earmarked reserve drawdown required
findings.quote: if the financial position can be brought back to a balanced position or better, this will be the first year since 2021/22 that the transfer of earmarked reserves to maintain the general fund at a prudent level (£14.6m from 2026/27) will not be required. This position aligns to the approved Reserves Strategy, which identifies the Council's required level of general balances as being £14.6m. It should be noted that the position at the end of Quarter 1 is already projecting a significant overspend and if the trend of previous years continues the use of earmarked reserves will again be necessary in 2026/27 to replenish general fund balances.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Savings delivery shortfall: only 70.87% of £5.579m savings forecast to be achieved, £1.625m at risk
findings.detail: Of £5.579m in approved budget savings, only £3.954m (70.87%) is forecast to be delivered in-year. £1.625m (29.13%) is at risk due to implementation delays. Only £0.401m of temporary mitigations have been identified for the slipped amount, leaving a gap of £1.224m. The report notes 'it is critical that action plans continue to be addressed and implemented to ensure that savings are delivered or alternative permanent reductions in expenditure are found.'
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls are a leading indicator of future budget stress. When a council can deliver only 71% of planned savings at Q1, it signals either weak planning, execution risk, or unachievable savings targets. This feeds into the overspend problem.
findings.figures: £5.579m total savings required; £3.954m (70.87%) on track; £1.625m (29.13%) at risk; £0.401m temporary mitigations; £1.224m unmitigated gap
findings.quote: Of the £1.625m of savings that have not yet been achieved, temporary mitigations of £0.401m have been identified / are in the process of being developed. Further work is needed to ensure these savings are delivered in full on a recurring basis to negate pressures on the current year and future years budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £12.793m in-year pressure from High Needs Block insufficient for EHCP demand
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £12.793m in-year DSG pressure driven by insufficient High Needs Block funding to meet the growing number of pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans. The council is 'actively engaged in progressing its local SEND Reform Plan' and expects to become eligible for High Needs Stability Funding, 'but at this stage, the forecast position assumes no impact from potential reform funding as details of the Authority's final approved reform plan and the associated financial implications are yet to be confirmed.' The statutory override protecting the General Fund ends 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: This is a growing national problem affecting many councils, but the scale here (£12.8m) and the council's dependence on a government reform funding decision that hasn't been confirmed represents a material contingent liability and structural sustainability risk. The statutory override ends in 2028.
findings.figures: £12.793m in-year DSG pressure; statutory override until 31 March 2028; growing EHCP numbers
findings.quote: High Needs funding primarily supports provision for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) who require additional support to access education. The underlying financial challenge remains that available funding within the High Needs Block is insufficient to meet current levels of demand, particularly given the continued growth in the number of pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs).

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Children & Young People portfolio overspend of £7.617m driven by uncontrolled external placement costs
findings.detail: The Children Looked After service is overspending by £5.070m due to the cost of external residential and fostering placements. Home to School Transport for SEND is overspending by £1.500m from increasing demand. Child Protection adds £0.938m. The report notes teams are 'looking at alternatives to provision working with partners to manage risk' but does not describe a credible plan to arrest the underlying cost trajectory.
findings.matters: This is demand-led spending the council cannot easily reduce without service redesign. Lenders track this closely as it indicates whether a council can manage its most volatile budget area. The scale (7.6% of portfolio budget) shows loss of financial control.
findings.figures: £7.617m Children & Young People overspend; £5.070m Children Looked After; £1.500m Home to School Transport SEND; £0.938m Child Protection
findings.quote: The most significant financial pressures continue to relate to the cost of placements for children looked after, particularly the use of external residential and fostering provision, which is forecasting a combined overspend of £7.451m.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Fifth consecutive year of budget overspend unless costs are controlled, with £5.617m pressure at Q1
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a net budget overspend of £5.617m after corporate underspends in the first quarter. The report explicitly warns that 'unless the Council can bring these costs under control by the end of the year, 2026/27 will be the 5th successive year the Council has overspent against its approved budget.' findings.quote: The statutory deadline for the submission of the draft Statement of Accounts was 30 June 2026. However, the Council did not submit and publish its draft accounts until 7 July 2026.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Cabinet approved £1.536m capital investment to reduce out-of-borough placement costs
findings.detail: St Helens Council has approved capital investment to repurpose the former Parr Library site to expand Mill Green Special School and is working with local schools to develop new SEND bases. The council states that places in these settings cost significantly less than out-of-borough alternatives.
findings.matters: This shows the council recognising the cost problem and attempting a structural solution (expand in-house capacity to displace expensive external placements), but the effectiveness and timeline of this strategy are untested against a £7m-per-year placement cost line.
findings.figures: £1.536m capital investment approved
findings.quote: St Helens Council's Cabinet have approved a £1.536m capital investment to repurpose and renovate the former Parr Library site to accommodate additional pupils at Mill Green Special School.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Even with High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the deficit, the council must find approximately £1.250m from its own resources
findings.detail: Subject to DfE approval of a SEND Reform Plan, the Authority will receive a High Needs Stability Grant in 2026/27 covering up to 90% of the accumulated deficit as at 31st March 2026. The council must identify measures to address the remaining 10% from within its own resources.
findings.matters: Government support is conditional and partial. The council faces a forced saving requirement on top of general budget pressures, and failure to approve the Reform Plan removes even that 90% cushion.
findings.figures: At least approximately £1.250m unfunded
findings.quote: Although this is positive news, the Authority will need to identify measures to address the remaining 10% from within its own resources and this would still be a significant pressure (currently, at least approximately £1.250m).

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Statutory override protecting DSG deficits from revenue impact expires in March 2028
findings.detail: Currently, DSG deficits do not impact the council's revenue budget due to a statutory override. This protection continues only until March 2028, at which point a £12.5m+ deficit could directly affect the council's general fund. The council will be working against a hard deadline.
findings.matters: After 2028, this deficit becomes a revenue budget problem for the council, not a separate DSG issue. A lender needs to know when statutory protection runs out.
findings.figures: March 2028
findings.quote: Under current arrangements and regulations set out in the Local Authorities (Capital Finance and Accounting) (England) Regulations, DSG deficits are held within a separate reserve and do not impact on the Council's revenue budget. This statutory override will continue until March 2028.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: Non-maintained and independent specialist placement costs escalated 84% in two years, from £9.613m to £17.731m
findings.detail: The paper documents rapid cost inflation in out-of-borough SEND placements. Costs rose from £9.613m in 2023/24 to £13.311m in 2024/25, then to £17.731m in 2025/26. This acceleration shows the cost driver is outpacing the council's ability to absorb it and signals either growing need or significant price inflation.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about a cost line growing this fast without a clear solution beyond external government funding.
findings.quote: Over the last two financial years, expenditure on these placements has increased from £9.613m in 2023/24, to £13.311m in 2024/25, and £17.731m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: DSG Outturn 25-26
findings.headline: High needs block deficit of £12.008m is described as financially unsustainable
findings.detail: The high needs block overspend is the primary driver of the overall £12.509m DSG deficit. Funding is insufficient to meet demand, particularly for pupils with EHCP who cannot be educated in mainstream settings. The council faces dual pressures: £7.131m for specialist non-maintained or independent provision placements, and £5.432m for high needs top-up payments to schools.
findings.matters: This is a material structural deficit in a statutory ring-fenced grant that signals persistent undersourcing of SEND provision and will become a general fund pressure when the statutory override expires in 2028.
findings.figures: £12.008m high needs block pressure; £7.131m specialist placements; £5.432m top-up payments
findings.quote: This level of pressure is financially unsustainable.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Regeneration portfolio £0.604m overspend from delayed sale of Lincoln House and Wesley House
findings.detail: The Regeneration portfolio shows overspend primarily driven by failure to deliver planned asset sales. The sale of Lincoln House and Wesley House, which were budgeted as cost reductions, have not been completed, indicating asset disposal strategy or valuation challenges.
findings.matters: Inability to complete planned asset sales to fund savings indicates potential asset management issues or overly optimistic budgeting, and signals risk to planned financial improvements.
findings.figures: £0.604m overspend in Regeneration (£0.700m at P2)
findings.quote: There is also a significant overspend within the Regeneration portfolio, with a forecast overspend of £0.604m, primarily because of the non-delivery of savings, in particular the delay in the sale of Lincoln House and Wesley House.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Adult Social Care & Health £1.5m overspend from ongoing demand and rising care package costs
findings.detail: Adult social care shows forecast overspend of £1.5m, worsening from £1.2m at Period 2. The driver is ongoing demand pressures and increases in the cost of individual care packages.
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures in an ageing population represent a structural budget challenge that cannot be easily reduced and may continue to deteriorate.
findings.figures: £1.5m overspend at P3 (£1.2m at P2)
findings.quote: The other main pressure is within Adult Social Care & Health, reflecting ongoing demand pressures and the increases in the cost of individual care packages.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Children & Young People services overspend doubled to £7.747m, driven by staffing and placement cost pressures
findings.detail: The Children & Young People portfolio shows the largest single overspend, more than double the Period 2 position. Drivers are social work staffing challenges, unachieved savings, and placement costs. Agency staff reduction plans are in place but implementation is slow, and Ofsted registration delays have hampered savings delivery.
findings.matters: Once social care placements are made, they are sticky costs difficult to reverse; doubling of this pressure in six months signals accelerating demand and cost control issues.
findings.figures: £7.747m overspend at P3 (£3.817m at P2); represents largest single portfolio pressure
findings.quote: The main pressure is within Children & Young People, the main drivers of this being social work staffing challenges, unachieved savings and placement costs. A plan is in place to reduce the reliance upon agency staff but this will take time to implement, and the delivery of savings has been hampered in this financial year due to delays in Ofsted registration.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of budget overspend, worsening from £3.119m to £5.448m
findings.detail: The council's forecast overspend has deteriorated at Period 3 compared to Period 2. External auditors Grant Thornton have flagged the council's financial position and made specific recommendations on financial management, indicating auditor concern about the trajectory.
findings.matters: A pattern of four consecutive years of overspend combined with audit concern signals persistent financial control issues and depleting reserves sustainability.
findings.figures: £5.448m net forecast overspend 2025/26; £3.119m at Period 2; portfolio overspend £9.117m against net budget of £203.172m
findings.quote: The forecast position has worsened compared to the overspend position within the 2025/26 FMR 2 and will result in a fourth consecutive year of overspend. Breaking the cycle of overspends is a key milestone for the Council's financial stability over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Council must begin to establish better control over demand-led spending in children's and adult social care
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer identifies a need to 'manage the demand and price pressures, specifically within children's services and adult social care, such that the Council can begin to better control its expenditure'. The phrasing 'begin to better control' indicates expenditure in these areas has not been well-controlled historically.
findings.matters: This is a critical condition for medium-term budget stability. If demand-led services continue to exceed budget, reserves will deplete rapidly and Section 114 risk will escalate.
findings.figures: Not quantified as separate budget line
findings.quote: To manage the demand and price pressures, specifically within children's services and adult social care, such that the Council can begin to better control its expenditure

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Borrowing capacity is explicitly constrained by revenue budget pressures; capital investment will be limited by affordability
findings.detail: The council states that 'the revenue budget position remains challenging' and that any capital borrowing 'will need to be carefully considered and the revenue impact remain affordable'. The capital programme exceeds £224m over three years but cannot assume unconstrained borrowing to fund it.
findings.matters: For lenders assessing debt capacity and covenant headroom, this signals the council's ability to borrow is limited. Capital priorities may be deferred or scaled, affecting long-term asset management.
findings.figures: Capital programme estimated value exceeds £224 million over 2026-2029
findings.quote: As the revenue budget position remains challenging, any increases to borrowing to fund schemes will need to be carefully considered and the revenue impact remain affordable.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: The council is dependent on the full 4.99% Council Tax increase; reducing it would increase likelihood of future service cuts
findings.detail: The council explicitly recommends the full 4.99% Council Tax increase (2% ASC precept plus 2.99% general increase). The paper warns that any reduction below this limit would have 'material consequences and increase the likelihood of future reductions in services', signalling this income is essential to budget balance and the council has no contingency if tax growth is restricted.
findings.matters: Revenue dependency on tax maximisation reduces resilience. Any variance in collection, policy constraint, or electorate resistance would immediately force further savings or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Band D Council Tax £1,975.65; total Council Tax Requirement £106.727 million
findings.quote: Any proposal to reduce the Council Tax uplift below the 4.99% referendum limit would have material consequences and increase the likelihood of future reductions in services.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult social care cost pressures are significant and public opposition to proposed savings is documented
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges 'significant budget pressure areas within services' with 'market pressures' particularly in social care, addressed through budget uplifts. However, consultation responses show the majority of residents found proposed savings in domiciliary care hours, mental health floating support, and adult respite services 'disagreeable'. The equality impact assessment identifies these will have 'potential cumulative negative impact on disabled and older people'.
findings.matters: Implementation risk: if savings cannot be delivered due to service quality issues, public pressure, or increased need, unplanned spending will destabilise the budget quickly. Demand-led services are difficult to control once political resistance emerges.
findings.figures: Not quantified in headline budget figures
findings.quote: Adult and Older People Social Care savings options linked to domiciliary care hours, Internal and external mental health floating support service, and the review of respite services for adults with a learning disability, were all felt to be disagreeable by the majority of respondents.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: The entire budget balance is conditional on full delivery of previously approved savings; no alternative is identified
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that savings are 'imperative' to deliver a balanced budget. The budget contains no growth and assumes all approved savings will be delivered in full during 2026/27 and the medium term. Failure to deliver any savings creates a gap with no identified alternative funding or service reduction mechanism.
findings.matters: If savings do not materialise as planned, the council will draw on reserves or seek Exceptional Financial Support. Budget dependency on prior approvals is a delivery and political risk that lenders must assess.
findings.figures: Council Tax Requirement £106.727 million (balanced on savings delivery)
findings.quote: It is imperative that the savings options agreed are progressed and delivered in 2026/27 and over the medium term in order to provide a budget that is balanced based on the current assumptions and projections.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Section 114 Notice risk is acknowledged as substantial and likely in the future if budget conditions fail
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly states that whilst the risk of issuing a Section 114 Notice is not imminent during this MTFS period, it is substantial and likely in the future. The risk materialises if any of three critical conditions fail: delivering approved savings, managing demand pressures in children's and adult social care, or identifying new efficiencies by 2028/29. Reserve depletion or Exceptional Financial Support would likely precede this.
findings.matters: A Section 114 Notice (statutory spending prohibition) is the most serious financial distress indicator. For lenders, it signals potential inability to service debt or meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Whilst the risk of the Council having to issue a Section 114 Notice is substantial i.e. it is likely in the future, it is not yet likely over the period of this Medium Term Financial Strategy.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review increases revenue nominally but does not increase actual spending power; Council Tax rise is still required to balance
findings.detail: The Commission notes that while government funding increased through the Fair Funding Review and changes to deprivation formulas, these gains are entirely consumed by cost increases the council faces. Previous ringfenced grants have been merged into general funding, creating a visual increase that masks no real fiscal gain. The council still requires a Council Tax rise to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Structural funding squeeze with no headroom for growth or investment; dependent on Council Tax increases to maintain service levels, which is politically and operationally constrained.
findings.figures: No specific percentages; described as merger of "previously ringfenced budgets into the base Grant."
findings.quote: The Commission understands the merging of previously ringfenced budgets into the base Grant give the appearance that the Council is receiving more funding but this is simply a repackaging of grants and there will still be a requirement to increase Council Tax rates to generate a balanced budget

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: 2026/27 is the final year of the current MTFS with minimal fiscal flexibility
findings.detail: The budget scrutiny focused on how the council would stick to the existing MTFS rather than proposing new initiatives, with explicit recognition that there is "little room within budgets for additional spending or savings" in this final year.
findings.matters: End of planning cycle creates uncertainty about the next MTFS; constrained flexibility now may lead to sharp adjustments when the new plan is set.
findings.figures: MTFS set by Council in March 2024; 2026/27 is year three of three.
findings.quote: with 2026/27 being the third and final year of the current MTFS there was little room within budgets for additional spending or savings, and every penny needed to be managed effectively

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: Council is experiencing overspends this year from demand in Children's and Adults' Social Care and SEN education
findings.detail: The Commission notes overspends have occurred in the current year and recognises persistent budget pressures from high demand in statutory social care services. These pressures arise from both increased demand and inflated external provision costs, which are difficult to mitigate given statutory duties.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends signal operational financial control weakness and whether demand growth is outpacing budget allocation.
findings.figures: No specific numbers given; report notes this is a year-on-year pattern.
findings.quote: The Commission notes the overspends that have occurred this year and recognises the persistent reasons for budget pressures from high levels of demand in Adults and Children's Social Care and SEN education provision

news_drafts.lead: A material overspend in a major service directorate signals budget control problems and pressure from demand that exceeds the council's savings capacity—both material risks for lenders assessing financial stability.
